svg.aria-label: Diagram: the four IPv4 addresses Google Cloud reserves in every subnet primary range named and explained, why only the gateway does a job today and why even it answers no ping, why the broadcast and second-to-last reservations are inherited convention rather than necessity as proved by secondary ranges reserving none, how IPv6 reserves two slash 96 ranges described only as system use, and why a fixed four-address overhead costs proportionally more the smaller the subnet
svg.title: The addresses reserved in every subnet: one job, two conventions, and a placeholder
svg.text: Four addresses are reserved in every primary range. One of them has a job.
Two are reserved for convention and for nothing yet, which is why secondary ranges reserve none.
The four, as the documentation lists them for 10.1.2.0/24
10.1.2.0 — network address, the first address in the primary IPv4 range.
10.1.2.1 — default gateway, the second address. The only one doing work.
10.1.2.254 — second-to-last: reserved by Google Cloud for POTENTIAL FUTURE USE.
10.1.2.255 — broadcast, the last address in the primary IPv4 range.
Four addresses, a fixed count, taken from every primary range on the network.
Only one has a job today, and it does not answer
The gateway is real: SDN reserves a virtual gateway IP for the primary range of each subnet.
But virtual gateways do not respond to ICMP traffic or decrement IP TTL headers — so it
will not answer ping and will not appear in traceroute.
The docs say to configure tools not to treat that inability as a failure condition.
The other two are inherited convention, and here is the proof
BROADCAST is reserved for a capability the network does not have: VPC networks do not
support broadcast or multicast addresses within the network. Unicast only.
SECOND-TO-LAST is reserved for potential future use — that is, for nothing yet.
Proof it is inheritance and not necessity: SECONDARY ranges reserve ZERO. Google lets you
use all addresses in them, and they have no reserved virtual gateway either.
IPv6 reserves differently, and that settles it
IPv6 reserves the FIRST and LAST /96 of the subnet internal /64 — two ranges, described
only as reserved for system use. No network address. No broadcast. No placeholder.
A /64 holds 4,294,967,296 ranges of /96, so the reservation is unmeasurable.
Where Google designed the addressing without inheriting IPv4 convention, the convention
vanished and only system use remained.
The cost is a FIXED four, so its proportional weight is set entirely by how small you cut.
A /29 loses 4 of 8 — fifty per cent. A /24 loses 4 of 256. Same overhead, different bill.
So the four reserved addresses are this block’s clearest argument for #63: fewer subnets,
larger ranges. Every boundary you draw pays the same toll, whatever the subnet is worth.
